item.title: Shivelyuch Socked In
item.summary: A cloud layer encircled the flanks of the volcano on the Kamchatka Peninsula but left its restless summit caldera in view.
item.page_text:
A cloud layer encircled the flanks of the volcano on the Kamchatka Peninsula but left its restless summit caldera in view.
In the same way that Shivelyuch (also called Shiveluch) frequently displays volcanic activity, it is also chronically obscured by clouds. When the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 captured this image on November 8, 2026, clouds encroached on the snowy mountain on Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula . But they hovered beneath the volcano’s 3,283-meter (10,771-foot) peak, leaving a clear opening over its caldera and northern upper slopes.
The upper reaches of Shivelyuch feature a caldera 9 kilometers (5.6 miles) wide that is open to the south. A lava dome , formed by vents extruding viscous magma, appears as a dark area within it. Lava domes on Shivelyuch go through cycles of growth and collapse, with collapses sometimes setting off fast-moving avalanches of hot ash and rock called pyroclastic flows .
In November 2026, effusive eruptions of lava and explosive activity at Shivelyuch had been ongoing for months , according to reports from the Kamchatka Volcanic Eruption Response Team (KVERT). And despite frequent cloudiness, satellites regularly detect thermal anomalies from the volcano.
On the day of this image, KVERT reported that a plume of resuspended ash drifted 120 kilometers (75 miles) to the east. That kind of activity is relatively tame for the mountain. Explosions from Shivelyuch periodically send ash several kilometers up into the atmosphere, where it can travel great distances and pose risks to aircraft . In July 2026, an ash plume rode the jet stream over the Bering Sea into Alaskan airspace, according to news reports , prompting the cancellation of multiple flights.
NASA Earth Observatory image by Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey . Story by Lindsey Doermann.

item.title: Entire villages cleared, river diverted as China builds world's largest dam on India's ...
item.summary: Fresh satellite imagery analysis by an Indian geospatial AI deep tech start-up incubated at FITT, IIT Delhi, shows construction of China's 60 GW ...
item.page_text:
(TibetanReview.net, Nov26’26) – China is on an all-out mode to build the world’s largest ever hydroelectric dam on Tibet’s Yarlung Tsangpo river on a location only 40-50 kilometres away from the border of India’s Arunachal Pradesh state. The site is known to be in a seismically active zone, raising serious concerns in downstream India.
Fresh satellite imagery analysis by an Indian geospatial AI deep tech start-up incubated at FITT, IIT Delhi, shows construction of China’s 60 GW Medog hydropower project on Yarlung Tsangpo (the Siang in India) is advanced and widespread, reported the timesofindia.com Nov 24.
It cited findings of a public-release assessment by EarthSense Labs as showing that entire villages had been cleared at the main dam site, river diversion works were visible and heavy industrial infrastructure had been built near the Arunachal Pradesh border.
The Chinese project is a multi-structure dam system along the lower Yarlung Tsangpo river in southeastern Tibet. It includes a tunnel across the river’s famous “Great U-Bend”, multiple power stations and outlets before the river enters India, the report said.
The assessment report is stated to list four critical locations and assets — a large dam near Mainling town, where “work has started extensively after July 2025”; a lower dam, possibly near Pai town; a tunnel through Namcha Barwa Mountain; and a tunnel outlet near the India-Tibet border, downstream of Medog County, where work has also started.
Developmental work on the tunnel outlet area is stated to have started even before the ground-breaking ceremony.
The project is planned as five cascade stations at an estimated cost of 1.2 trillion yuan (roughly $168 billion). It would use tunnels of around 40 km to exploit a river drop of more than 2,000 metres over a stretch of about 50 km, the assessment report has said.
EarthSense Labs’ study of imagery from Jul 2025 was stated to show villages and farm fields at the site of the proposed Mainling high dam; that by Dec 2025, the villages were cleared, the fields removed and earthwork begun.
Imagery of Aug 2026 was stated to show diversion works, the relocation of entire villages and the emergence of new roads, makeshift housing and office buildings on the north bank.
The key finding, according to the assessment report, was “Site clearance and earthwork after Jul 2025, followed by river diversion works by Aug 2026.”
The assessment report documents the scale and pace of construction but does not quantify environmental damage, downstream flow effects or risks to Arunachal Pradesh and Assam. Its locations are described as indicative, and the analysis relies on satellite imagery, the report said.

item.title: Japan's solar farms on cleared forest: a satellite map of 139 sites since 2024 | Orteliana
item.summary: Satellite images show at least 662 hectares of Japanese forest turned ... Satellite images: Copernicus Sentinel-2 (contains modified Copernicus Sentinel ...
item.page_text:
Every month, we look for new solar plants in satellite images of Japan and check whether the land was forest before. Between January 2024 and November 2026, we found 139 sites where solar plants were built on former forest, and checked each one by hand. Together they cover about 662 hectares, or more than 900 soccer fields.
Sendatsuyama, Fukushima · 2017 to 2026 · Copernicus Sentinel-2
Sendatsuyama, a hill near the city of Fukushima, one satellite image a year from 2017 to 2026. Each frame combines images from April to November, so work that began in November 2021 first shows in 2022. By 2024 the hillside was bare. Panels went in during 2025. Our map detected the plant on 27 March that year.
Japan’s solar capacity grew fast after the country introduced a feed-in tariff in 2012. With little flat land, developers often cleared mountain forest to make room for solar plants. According to data from the Agency for Natural Resources and Energy , forest development and logging for solar power, counting both permits and notices, came to about 13,000 cases and 19,000 hectares between fiscal 2013 and 2020.
Cleared slopes are more likely to slide in heavy rain. In the July 2018 floods in western Japan, 19 solar plants of 50 kilowatts or more reported accidents, and the economy ministry found that landslides caused 11 of them. Disputes over landscapes and wildlife have also set residents against developers in many places.
At Sendatsuyama in Fukushima, work began in November 2021 on a site of about 345 hectares for a plant of roughly 40 megawatts, according to Fukushima Prefecture’s environmental assessment records . The bare slopes are visible from the city, and in August 2023 the city of Fukushima issued a “No More Megasolar” declaration against further large solar farms.
Around the Kushiro wetland in Hokkaido, home to rare wildlife, solar construction drew national attention. In March 2026, the Hokkaido Shimbun reported that the prefecture had found arsenic and two other hazardous substances above legal limits in soil at a planned site.
In Kamogawa, Chiba, construction of a plant of about 100 megawatts, with a forest development permit for about 146 hectares, began in May 2025, prefectural records show . In October 2025, Chiba Prefecture found that about 2.4 hectares of forest, across 13 spots that the permit required the developer to keep, had been cut. Kyodo News reported in May 2026 that there was still no prospect of restoring them .
The hills of Kamogawa, Chiba, in 2024 and 2026, in the same frame. Drag the line to compare them. Slopes that were forest in 2024 had been cleared on a large scale by 2026.
In December 2025, a ministerial meeting adopted a package of measures on large solar projects . An amended Forest Act took effect in April 2026. Breaking the conditions of a forest development permit can now bring up to three years in prison or a fine of up to ¥3 million. Developers who ignore orders can also be named publicly.
In March 2026, the Forestry Agency told prefectures that developments on 40 hectares of forest or more should keep about 60% of it. The same month, the economy ministry decided that ground-mounted commercial solar will no longer get feed-in tariff or premium support from fiscal 2027. Local governments had passed 344 ordinances restricting solar installations by April 2026, according to the Research Institute for Local Government .
These rules make it more important to know where and when a plant replaced forest. Yet Japan’s statistics on forest development only give totals by fiscal year and prefecture.
Orteliana looks for new solar plants in images from Sentinel-2, a pair of European satellites that photograph Japan every few days. For each plant we find, our map shows before-and-after images and whether the land was forest, and we update it every month.
Of the new solar sites on our map from January 2024 to November 2026, 139 were built on land that was forest. We checked each of them on satellite and aerial images. Together they cover about 662 hectares, or 6.6 square kilometers. That’s more than 900 soccer fields.
Of the 139 sites, 57, or about four in ten, are in three prefectures north of Tokyo. Fukushima has 24 of them, Ibaraki 17 and Tochigi 16.
The 28.2-hectare site at Sendatsuyama is the second largest of the 139. The table shows the five largest.
Our map detected the Sendatsuyama plant on 27 March 2025. It counts the plant as two sites, of 28.2 and 14.4 hectares, and both were on former forest.
Japan’s Forest Act asks the national government, prefectures and municipalities to set forest plans for how forests are managed and protected. In private forests under a prefecture’s regional forest plan, clearing more than 0.5 hectares for solar power needs the governor’s permit. The threshold was 1 hectare until April 2023.
Since February 2026, the Forestry Agency has published a map of these forests as open data. When we laid it over the 139 sites, 97 overlapped forest plan areas, all of them private forest. At Sendatsuyama, about 11.7 hectares of the 28.2-hectare site overlap private forest.
Open the map of new solar farms in Japan and you’ll see every new plant we’ve found since January 2024 as a dot. Orange dots mark plants built on former forest, and blue dots plants built on farmland, grassland or open land.
Use chart 1 to pick a period and chart 2 to pick a size range. Button 3, “Former forest only”, hides everything except plants on former forest. Type a place name or coordinates into the search box at 4.
Click a dot and the plant’s details appear on the right: its detection date, area, previous land use and overlap with forest plan areas.
Drag the line across the two satellite images to compare the previous summer’s image with the latest one. Tick “Forest plan areas” under the images to shade those forests on top.
In this recording, we filter to plants on former forest and open the Sendatsuyama plant. After comparing the two images, we tick “Forest plan areas”

item.title: A remote island in New Zealand was supposed to be a safe haven for wildlife - AOL.com
item.summary: A landscape shaped by glaciers. The image was captured on December 12, 2025, by the Operational Land Imager aboard the Landsat 9 satellite. Resolution ...
item.page_text:
Today’s Image of the Day from NASA Earth Observatory features Resolution Island, a remote expanse of wilderness off the southwestern coast of New Zealand.
Surrounded by deep blue waters and covered in dense vegetation, the island appears to be an ideal sanctuary for wildlife.
Its isolation, however, has not always offered the protection that conservationists envisioned.
For more than a century, Resolution Island has been at the center of an ambitious effort to preserve some of New Zealand’s most extraordinary native birds.
Its history reveals both the potential and the limitations of using islands as natural barriers against invasive species.
The image was captured on December 12, 2025, by the Operational Land Imager aboard the Landsat 9 satellite.
Resolution Island lies within Fiordland National Park, a spectacular region of mountains, forests, waterfalls, and narrow waterways that extend deep into the southwestern coast of New Zealand’s South Island.
During past ice ages, enormous glaciers moved through the region, gradually carving deep valleys into the landscape.
As the glaciers retreated and sea levels rose, ocean water flooded many of these valleys, creating the dramatic fjords visible today.
Resolution Island is the largest island within the national park. Its mountainous terrain reaches an elevation of 3,507 feet at the summit of Mount Clerke.
The island’s varied landscape supports wetlands, ancient evergreen forests, and high-elevation grasslands. These distinct environments provide a range of habitats for native wildlife.
New Zealand’s long geographical isolation allowed wildlife to evolve in remarkable ways.
Before humans arrived, the country had virtually no native land mammals other than bats. Birds occupied many ecological niches that mammals filled elsewhere in the world.
Some species gradually lost the ability to fly, while others developed behaviors that left them particularly vulnerable to ground-dwelling predators.
Among them were kiwi, which forage along the forest floor, and kākāpō, the world’s only flightless parrot.
For millions of years, these birds survived without facing the kinds of mammalian predators found on other continents.
That evolutionary advantage became a liability when people introduced unfamiliar animals into New Zealand’s ecosystems.
Rats, cats, and members of the weasel family brought new pressures that native birds were poorly equipped to withstand.
By the nineteenth century, the decline of New Zealand’s native wildlife was becoming increasingly apparent.
European settlers had introduced stoats and other predators in an attempt to control rabbit populations. Instead, these animals created another ecological problem by preying on vulnerable native species.
In 1872, conservationist Thomas Henry Potts suggested that Resolution Island could provide a refuge for birds threatened by introduced predators.
The surrounding ocean appeared to offer a natural protective barrier, allowing native species to survive without the dangers they faced on the mainland.
Resolution Island became a protected reserve in 1891, making it part of a pioneering chapter in New Zealand’s conservation history.
Long before modern wildlife restoration programs existed, naturalists were experimenting with ideas that would eventually become central to endangered species management.
One of the most dedicated figures in this undertaking was Richard Henry, who became the island’s caretaker.
Henry recognized the urgency of protecting birds that were rapidly disappearing from other parts of the country.
Working in an isolated and physically demanding environment, he transported hundreds of native birds across the waters of Fiordland.
More than 700 birds , primarily kiwi and kākāpō, were relocated to Resolution Island and neighboring islands during his conservation efforts.
Much of the work involved traveling by rowboat through a region known for challenging weather and rugged terrain.
Henry’s efforts represented an early attempt to prevent extinction by establishing wildlife populations in geographically isolated locations.
Unfortunately, the assumption that the surrounding waters would keep predators away proved incorrect.
By 1900, invasive predators had been detected on Resolution Island. Stoats were capable of swimming across the channels that separated the island from nearby land.
The discovery undermined years of painstaking conservation work and exposed a weakness in the island’s natural defenses.
Stoats are highly adaptable hunters. Their ability to exploit different environments makes them particularly problematic in New Zealand, where many native birds nest on or near the ground.
Henry attempted to control the invading predators through trapping but eventually left the island to pursue conservation work elsewhere.
His experience demonstrated that geographical isolation alone was not necessarily enough to protect vulnerable species.
More than a century later, conservationists continue to build on Henry’s original vision.
In 2008, New Zealand’s Department of Conservation launched a predator management program on Resolution Island to improve the prospects of native wildlife.
Maintaining such a program across a large, mountainous island presents considerable challenges.
Dense forests, steep slopes, and remote locations complicate efforts to monitor wildlife and control invasive animals.
Conservation also extends into the surrounding waters, where a marine reserve protects coastal ecosystems near the island’s distinctive Five Fingers Peninsula.
Viewed from space, Resolution Island offers a striking portrait of an apparently untouched wilderness.
Yet beneath its forest canopy lies a complex ecological history shaped by human intervention, invasive species, and generations of conservation work.
The island remains a powerful reminder that protecting nature sometimes requires far more than simply setting it aside.

item.title: Mapping the Iowa Lead Explosion
item.summary: Yesterday the US Army carried out a controlled detonation of 68 drums of degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant near Middletown, Iowa. The stockpile contained approximately 9,500 pounds of an explosive compound, which had deteriorated and become increasingly dangerous to handle. Although controlled detonation was considered the safest way to dispose of the material, the explosion presented another potential hazard: releasing toxic lead dust into the atmosphere. Depending on wind direction and weather conditions, airborne particles could travel considerable distances before settling on farmland, waterways and nearby communities. Two interesting interactive maps have been created to explore where this pollution might travel. Where the Lead Will Go The first map, Where the Lead Will Go , attempts to simulate the movement of millions of airborne particles using weather forecasts. Users can move through five days of predictions, or press play to watch the simulated dust cloud travel across the landscape. Different colour bands distinguish between lead remaining airborne and lead that has settled on the ground. You can also switch between scenarios in which 100%, 50% or 10
